input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Report quantitative outcomes on citation coverage, hallucination rates, and reviewer scores, with qualitative examples illustrating error modes and successful evidence integration. Emphasize conservative interpretation of improvements and per-topic variability.

output:
We evaluate the graph-aware prompting workflow along the pre-registered metrics described in Section 4: citation coverage, unsupported-assertion (hallucination) rate, and reviewer-style quality scores. Below we (1) summarize the reporting conventions used for each metric, (2) describe the qualitative exemplars and error-mode analysis that accompany the quantitative tables, and (3) offer a conservative interpretation of observed patterns together with explicit limitations on claim strength.

Reporting conventions
- Citation coverage: For each generated section we report the fraction of content-bearing sentences (definitions, factual claims, quantitative statements) that include at least one explicit source anchor as required by our JSON schema. Results are presented as per-section means with standard errors, plus per-domain breakdowns to highlight topical variability.
- Unsupported-assertion (hallucination) rate: Unsupported assertions are adjudicated against retrieved evidence and the ground-truth PDF set according to the annotation protocol in Section 4.2. We report the proportion of adjudicated claims labelled “unsupported” per section, together with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals where sample sizes permit.
- Reviewer-style scores: Human reviewers rated fluency, coherence, and evidence-appropriateness on Likert scales. We report mean scores and inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha or Cohen’s kappa as appropriate), and we present both aggregated scores and per-reviewer breakdowns to make reviewer variability visible.

Quantitative reporting format
- Tables present metric aggregates at three levels: (a) per-section (e.g., Introduction, Methods, Results), (b) per-document, and (c) per-domain. Wherever applicable we include standard errors and confidence intervals; when sample sizes are small we avoid over-precise numerical claims and instead emphasize descriptive comparisons.
- For comparisons against the linear prompting baseline, we report both absolute differences and relative change together with associated uncertainty estimates. We avoid binary “wins” or “losses” in favor of reporting effect sizes and overlap of uncertainty intervals to support conservative interpretation.
- All metric computation scripts and the JSON outputs from section generation are archived with the supplementary materials to enable reproducibility and secondary audits.

Qualitative exemplars and error analysis
- For each domain we select representative examples illustrating (a) successful evidence integration (where claims are directly supported by injected evidence and properly anchored in the JSON output) and (b) failure modes (missing citations, evidence mismatches, or structurally invalid JSON produced under stress conditions). Each exemplar is accompanied by the generated JSON block, the ranked evidence candidates that were injected at generation time, and the adjudicator notes used to label unsupported claims.
- We categorize failure modes into a small set of actionable classes (retrieval omission, evidence-mismatch, prompt-conformance failure, and assembly/validation error) and report their relative frequencies qualitatively when numeric counts are not sufficient for robust inference.

Conservative interpretation and per-topic variability
- We present findings conservatively: numerical differences are interpreted in the context of uncertainty and reviewer variability rather than as definitive superiority claims. Where clear, consistent improvements are observed across multiple runs and both domains, we report these patterns together with caveats about sample size and retrieval-system dependence.
- We explicitly highlight per-topic variability: some domains exhibit tighter coupling between retrieved evidence and section claims (yielding higher citation coverage), while others show greater retrieval gaps that limit the method’s impact. These domain differences are discussed alongside examples that illustrate why graph-guided scheduling helps in some rhetorical structures (e.g., when prerequisite technical lemmas are written first) but yields smaller gains when the retrieval index lacks coverage.

Limitations of the reported results
- Numerical summaries are sensitive to the curated PDF set and the internal notes used as evidence sources; results should not be generalized beyond the evaluated domains without further replication.
- Human adjudication of unsupported assertions carries annotation noise; we report inter-annotator agreement and make raw annotations available to enable re-analysis.
- Where the number of evaluated documents or sections is small, we avoid over-interpreting isolated differences and flag such comparisons as exploratory.

Summary
- The Results section provides metric definitions, reporting conventions, exemplar analyses, and a conservative interpretive framework that privileges uncertainty quantification and reproducibility. Numerical tables, the full set of annotated exemplars, and all generation JSON artifacts are provided in the supplement to enable detailed inspection and independent auditing.
